edbDesc: (or Faraday Ripples) Nonlinear standing waves that appear on liquids enclosed by a vibrating receptacle. When the vibration frequency exceeds a critical value, the flat hydrostatic surface becomes unstable. The waves can take the form of stripes, close-packed hexagons, or even squares or quasiperiodic patterns.
title: Faraday waves
description: Shake a dish of liquid up and down fast enough and its surface breaks into a standing pattern of squares, stripes or hexagons that bob at half the shaking rate. Faraday described them in 1831. Shake much faster and the crests fling off fine droplets, which is how ultrasonic humidifiers and nebulisers make mist.
effect: vibrating a container makes its liquid surface form standing wave patterns that can throw off droplets
usedIn: Arranging cells and particles into patterns for tissue engineering
strength: Patterns appear once the dish is shaken a bit harder than gravity; at 1.7 million shakes a second the crests throw off droplets a few micrometres across.
pickWhy: Specific named effect with a clear atomising job; not in the deck.
